:topic/_next.:topic/title: Double Integrals in Plane Polar Coordinates

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{z-x+y^2}} \: \textrm{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=1+x+y^2$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $-1 \leq y \leq 1.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 1,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z-x+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1+x+{y}^{2})-x+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2(1+2{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
![](images/d8/d8675cb0c59ba915cefe4b0bbe539f1e7e38b5a3ac2fae4bd2bb25e4de96e116.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} x^2y \: \textrm{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\sqrt2x-y$ and whose domain is a semicircle of radius $1$ centered at $O$ in the upper-half plane, as shown above.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(\sqrt2x-y) = \sqrt2,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\sqrt2x-y) = -1.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{1+(\sqrt{2})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,[\frac{{r}^{5}}{5}]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{[-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=xz,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=x^2-y$ for $0 \leq x \leq 2$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 
![](images/69/69764cda6db58d51cf12ab33a352191513d3f572292203135108bfc15f902584.svg)

What is the missing expression?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2-y) = 2x,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2-y) = -1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(2x)}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,x({x}^{2}-y)\sqrt{2+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,({x}^{3}-xy)\sqrt{2+4{x}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${\color{blue} (x^3-xy) \sqrt{2+4x^2}}.$
